source.title: Local Intrinsic Dimension of Representations Predicts Alignment and Generalization in AI Models and Human Brain
source.authors: Jun-Jie Yu; Wenxiao Ma; Chen Wei; Jian-Yu Zhang; Hao-Tian Deng; Zihan Deng; Quan-Ying Liu

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: It measures representation alignment with held-out ridge-regression prediction scores and examines how alignment relates to generalization, model scale, and architecture. This is a conceptual test of convergence, not a reproduction of the original method.
record.gate_note: The study reports AI–AI alignment results and their relationships with performance, architecture, and scale. It also reports extensive AI–brain alignment and dimensionality analyses; results that only measure AI–brain alignment or dimensionality without directly measuring AI–AI alignment are not included as rows. Results cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study measures AI–AI alignment (held-out ridge-regression R² between embeddings) across about 51 pretrained vision models. It relates that alignment to ImageNet performance, parameter count, pretraining-data size and architecture family. This is a different method aimed at V1's question.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Add that the authors find AI–AI alignment strongly shaped by architectural family while local intrinsic dimension is architecture-agnostic. They interpret convergence among high performers through flat minima, which they say is stronger within an architecture.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a vision-model and fMRI analysis with held-out ridge-regression embedding prediction, performance comparisons, and intrinsic-dimension analyses; it does not reproduce the original study's method. The paper also examines model capacity, training-data scale, and architecture.
record.method_sensitivity: AI–AI alignment is substantially higher within architectural families than across families. The paper also reports that correlations between intrinsic dimensionality and alignment/generalization weaken, and may change sign, as neighborhood scale increases; this varies the dimensionality analysis rather than the AI–AI alignment measure itself.

fits_no_version.finding: Reference-based AI–AI alignment correlates significantly with AI–brain (fMRI, NSD) alignment, within ConvNeXt and across architectures, subjects and ROIs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Models that converge with each other also converge with human visual cortex representations.

fits_no_version.finding: Lower local intrinsic dimension (small K) correlates with stronger AI–AI alignment. The correlation weakens or flips sign at large K.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representational convergence is predicted by low local intrinsic dimension of embeddings.

record.problems: The main results are largely qualitative in the supplied text: figure-based correlations and alignment scores are not reported numerically, and their coefficients and p-values are not stated. The study focuses on vision models and visual cortex; its text identifies language and audition as future extensions. Cross-architecture results show lower alignment across families, and the study does not isolate a common-reality explanation from training or architectural factors.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's individual-model AI–brain alignment tables and subject/region analyses are omitted where they do not report AI–AI alignment. Intrinsic-dimension-versus-alignment correlations across neighborhood scales and estimators are omitted because the AI–AI alignment measure itself is not varied; this is not a direct test of V6 as worded. No other direct AI–AI alignment result bearing on the tested versions was left out.

untested.parts: Non-vision and multimodal models; scaling across different architectures is not separated from within-family scaling; no numeric effect sizes.
All of it: no vision–language paired-data comparison.
All of it: no seed comparisons.
All of it. Ridge R² is used only as a similarity score, with no low-loss mapping, stitching, relative or unpaired test.
All of it: no feature- or circuit-level comparison.
The AI–AI similarity measure, its settings and the input distribution are never varied. Only the dimensionality estimator's K and estimator are varied.
Plateauing, and whether shared data or objectives explain convergence, are not tested.

missing.what: Pooling models across architectures 'slightly reduces' the alignment–performance correlations relative to within-architecture analyses, though they stay significant.
Pairwise AI–AI matrix ordered by brain alignment shows a coherent high-alignment block among top models and heterogeneous alignment among weaker ones.
Single-architecture analyses for ResNet and ResMLP show the same alignment–performance trends.

record.verdict_notes: All AI–AI results are figure-based, without numbers or coefficients. The reference model is a CLIP-LAION ConvNeXt, so cross-family 'convergence' means closeness to one ConvNeXt. V4 links were removed because the ridge R² serves only as a similarity measure. No original source is involved.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests vision models across performance, architecture, parameter count, and pretraining-data scale. It does not test convergence across modalities generally or establish that all differences in objectives and data are controlled.
No paired image-and-caption representation comparison between vision and language models is reported.
No comparison across random initializations or shared-seed feature/subspace analysis is reported.

The study uses ridge regression to predict one model's embeddings from another's and reports alignment scores, but does not establish that mappings are generally low-loss, linear maps across layers, stitchable, relative, or unpaired.
No recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits are compared across models.
The study varies intrinsic-dimension estimation scale and estimator, but does not vary the AI–AI similarity measure or its settings, or test out-of-distribution inputs for AI–AI convergence.

The study reports architecture-dependent alignment and effects of model/data scale, but does not establish that alignment plateaus, quantify how far it is from complete, or isolate shared objectives or training data as the cause rather than a common model of reality.

relationships.condition: ConvNeXt models grouped by ImageNet performance, parameter count and data size; cross-architecture alignment to the top reference
relationships.reason: Within-group alignment rises monotonically with performance (R1). Alignment to the reference tracks performance, including across families (R2, R5). Larger models and data give stronger alignment (R7, R8). All results are qualitative or significance-only.
relationships.display_finding: Alignment increased with performance within groups and across families, while larger models and larger training datasets also showed stronger alignment.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: ConvNeXt models grouped by ImageNet performance, parameter count and data size; cross-architecture alignment to the top reference
source_check.reason: R1 and R2 report stronger alignment with performance; R5 extends the association across architectures; R7 and R8 report stronger alignment with model and data scale. These support V1 in the tested settings without independently isolating architecture, objective and data differences.

relationships.condition: Pairwise alignment between different architecture families (ViT, ConvNeXt, ResNet, ResMLP)
relationships.reason: Models cluster by family, and across-family alignment is substantially lower than within-family alignment. Authors say high performance only 'partially' bridges architectures (R4).
relationships.display_finding: Models cluster by architecture family, with substantially lower alignment across families, and higher performance only partially bridges these differences.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Pairwise alignment between different architecture families (ViT, ConvNeXt, ResNet, ResMLP)
source_check.reason: R4 reports substantially weaker cross-family alignment and distinct within-family clusters; higher performance only partially bridges architectural differences.

relationships.reason: Convergence is incomplete and structured by architecture family. Authors attribute within-family alignment to shared parameter symmetries and optimization landscapes, not a common reality (R4). The shared-data cause is not tested.
relationships.display_finding: Alignment clustered within architectural families, which the authors attributed to shared parameter symmetries and optimization landscapes; shared training data was not tested as a cause.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: R4 supports the incomplete, architecture-structured convergence component of V7. Shared-data or shared-objective causation is untested. The flat-minima explanation is interpretive, and the authors do not establish that a common model of reality is excluded.
